\title{Given the File Being Changed, What Else Should Be Read?}
\subtitle{Import Structure, Issue Text and What the Issue Gives Away}

\author{Neil Lunavat}
\affiliation{%
  \institution{Pimpri Chinchwad College of Engineering}
  \country{India}}
\email{neillunavat3192@gmail.com}

\begin{abstract}
An agent editing one file of an unfamiliar repository must choose what else to read: the
median pull request here is made against 286{,}385 tokens of code, of which the files it needs
are 2.98\%. Given the file being changed, we compare two signals for that choice --- proximity
in the import graph and the words of the issue report --- and their fusion, on 2{,}412 change
tasks from 1{,}162 pull requests in 112 Python repositories. Each ordering is scored by how much
of an answer key it covers per line read, against two keys we never merge: the files co-edited
in the pull request, and the files defining symbols the change uses.

Two findings survive our controls. First, what the issue is worth depends on whether it names
a file the change touches. In 40.2\% of tasks it names one as code; there the issue is worth
0.156 AUC to the best fusion, against 0.016 elsewhere. Deleting from the same issue only what
points at the files --- their names, then their directories, then the symbols they define ---
accounts for 0.061 to 0.078 of that 0.140 difference, and the rest survives every redaction;
on seven repositories outside the sample the names alone mattered less, and not significantly
on the co-edited key. A benchmark built from issue reports therefore averages an easy regime with a hard one, and a
gain from issue-aware retrieval that is not reported per regime cannot be interpreted. Second,
fusing a length-aware personalised walk with issue-to-path matching is the robust choice: on
the pull requests that carry both keys it is never significantly worse than the best single
signal under any stratification, and it held on seven repositories outside the sample, scored
against predictions committed in advance. The exception is single-file changes, where the walk
alone is better. The two-hop import neighbourhood, the usual argument for graph retrieval,
holds 87.5\% of the needed files and also half the repository.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{code search, context retrieval, dependency graphs, software maintenance, empirical
software engineering}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

An agent is handed a bug report and a file to change. Before it can write anything it must
decide what else to read, and it cannot simply read everything. In the corpus we study the
median pull request is made against a repository of 286{,}385 tokens --- counting the
Python files in the import graph, excluding tests and non-Python files --- and 74.8\% of pull
requests are made against a repository larger than a 128{,}000-token window, 60.5\% against
one larger than 200{,}000. Meanwhile the files that carry the answer are a median 2.98\% of
the repository. The reduction available is roughly
34$\times$, and every line spent on an irrelevant file is a line not spent on a relevant
one. Something has to choose, and the choice is the subject of this paper.

The question is narrower than an agent's whole problem.
Every task here hands the reader the file being changed; the question is what \emph{else} to
read. We measure retrieval, not repair --- no agent is run --- and the corpus comes from
benchmarks that select for reproducible, test-verified fixes. Each of these is stated again
where it bears on a result, but together they mean this paper answers ``given the right file,
what else belongs in the context'', not how well an agent that must also find that file will
do.

A human faces a softer version of the same problem --- attention rather than tokens --- and
we return to that reading in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}. The budget is what makes the
question sharp, so we pose it in those terms throughout.

The dominant answer in tool building is the dependency graph. Aider builds a repository map
from the call and definition graph; RepoGraph, LocAgent and CoSIL construct code graphs and
walk them outward from a starting point. The premise is intuitive and rarely stated: what
you need to read is near, in the graph, to what you are changing.

There is a second signal, and it is the one a human reaches for first. Asked to fix the
login page, a developer thinks of the authentication files --- not because \m{login.py}
imports them, which it may well not, but because the words match. That signal sits in the
issue report.

We are not the first to notice it. SWE-bench's own sparse-retrieval baseline is BM25 with
the issue as the query~\cite{jimenez2024swebench}, Agentless~\cite{xia2025agentless} leans on
file and directory names, and the agentic systems all read the issue text as part of their
loop. What is missing is not the idea that words help. It is a measurement of how far they
carry against structure, on a stated answer key, under a stated budget, and with the issue
corpus's habit of naming the answer controlled for. Every system in Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys}
reports end-to-end accuracy against a single key, and none reports that comparison. That
issues often name the file to change is known: Agentless's manual pass over SWE-bench
Lite~\cite{xia2025agentless}
found that around half of its issues give the location of the file to edit, and models can
name the buggy file from the issue alone often enough to raise questions of
memorisation~\cite{liang2025illusion}. What has not been measured is how much of a retrieval
method's score that accounts for, which is what a benchmark average hides.

This paper compares the two, and the comparison needs a definition of which files a change
needed. We use two that can be recovered without human labelling: the files \emph{co-edited}
in the same pull request, and the files that \emph{define symbols} the changed code references;
and we check both against a third, annotated by people, on a separate set of tasks.
Graded as they come, the two keys rank the methods differently. Most of that difference is not
about the signals. A symbol key exists for a single-file change and a co-edited key does not,
so the two are scored on different pull requests; and in two tasks in five the issue names a
changed file outright, which a method matching issue words against file paths can simply read.
Every comparison that follows is therefore also reported on the pull requests that carry both
keys, and within strata of how explicitly the issue names its files, with the repository as the
statistical unit.

With those controls in place two findings remain, and the paper is organised around them. The
first concerns the benchmark more than the methods: issue-aware retrieval is worth far more on
issues that name their files, and a within-task redaction experiment measures how much of that
is the names themselves. We call the names \emph{leakage} only in this benchmark sense. In
deployment an issue that names \texttt{core.py} is a legitimate input; the problem is that an
average over issues that do and issues that do not describes neither, and the share of each
varies by corpus. The second finding is a recommendation: fusing a walk from the file with
issue-to-path matching is robust across both keys, every stratum, an external set of
repositories and a human-annotated key, and it survives the loss of the free seed ---
except for single-file changes, where the walk alone is better. Whether the walk should
favour short files depends on how a context is paid for, and we show both cases.

\subsection*{Research questions}

\begin{description}
\item[RQ1] How much of a repository is the seed's two-hop neighbourhood, and how much recall
does it buy over a same-sized random sample?
\item[RQ2] Do structural and lexical reading orders rank differently under the two evidence
sources, and by how much?
\item[RQ3] How much does conditioning on the seed file add over a query-independent
repository prior, and does the answer depend on the evidence source?
\item[RQ4] Do the two signals retrieve the same files, or different ones?
\item[RQ5] Does fusing them produce an ordering that is good under both evidence sources?
\item[RQ6] What fraction of tasks could be solved at all under a given budget --- that is,
how far is the best ordering we test from one that cannot be improved on?
\item[RQ7] How much of what issue text contributes is the issue naming the answer? When an
issue names a key file as code, and when it does not, what does an ordering gain from reading
the issue at all?
\item[RQ8] Do the answers survive a different cost rule, a human-annotated key, a dense
retriever, and the loss of the free seed?
\end{description}

RQ7 and RQ8 were not in the design freeze; RQ7 grew out of the leakage control, which was,
and RQ8 out of review. Section~\ref{sec:design-freeze} lists every analysis added after the
freeze, and which of them were tested against predictions committed in advance.

\subsection*{Contributions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A decomposition of what issue text is worth.} An issue-free twin of each fusion
gives the issue's total value, and three nested within-task redactions give the part carried by
what points at the key files. On issues that name a key file as code the issue is worth
$+0.156$ AUC to the best fusion, of which $0.061$ to $0.078$ is attributable to the names,
depending on how much beyond the filename is deleted (Section~\ref{sec:issue}).
\item \textbf{A robust recommendation, tested three ways.} Reciprocal-rank fusion of a
personalised walk with issue-to-path matching is never significantly worse than the best pure
ordering on the matched population. It held under predictions committed before scoring on seven
unseen repositories (where one of four predictions, about redaction, failed) and against
ContextBench's human-annotated key (all four held), and it remains the best ordering when the
file to change is not given but guessed from the issue (Section~\ref{sec:seedless}). Whether
the walk should be length-aware depends on how reading is charged: by lines it should, and two
fusions differing only in that are $0.042$ and $0.050$ AUC apart; charged per file, it should
not (Section~\ref{sec:metric}).
\item \textbf{Three controls for this kind of comparison}, each of which changed a conclusion
here: stratifying by whether the issue names a key file as code (40.2\% of tasks do); matching
the populations two keys are scored on (a co-edited key needs a multi-file change); and taking
the repository as the unit, which leaves the headline comparisons significant but changes the
significance verdict on 104 of 1{,}300: 102 of the 1{,}076 comparisons significant with the pull
request as the unit lose significance, 2 gain it, and none changes sign.
\item \textbf{Three corrections to common arguments for graph retrieval.} The two-hop
neighbourhood holds 87.5\% of the needed files and 56\% of the repository, at a median precision
of 3.4\%. Direction matters in one way only: walking against import edges is costly, while
discarding direction costs nothing measurable. And the advantage structure shows on a key
derived from imports is not corroborated by a human-annotated one: on the context a fix reads
but does not edit, which is what a walk is claimed to find, walks and issue text are
indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:contextbench}).
\item \textbf{A cost accounting and a replication package.} Python source runs to 8.50 tokens
per line; an oracle fits the whole key within 8{,}000 lines for 97.5\% of pull requests. Given its answer keys, the package rebuilds the study from a clean checkout and reproduces
every committed score exactly; rebuilding the symbol keys themselves on another machine changes
41 of 1{,}886 and no conclusion (Section~\ref{sec:threats}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background and Related Work}

\paragraph{Dependency structure as a guide to change.} Using program structure to decide what
a change touches is old. Impact analysis~\cite{bohner1996impact} propagates from a changed
element along dependencies; Robillard~\cite{robillard2008topology} ranks program elements by
the topology of their dependencies; feature-location surveys~\cite{dit2013featurelocation} catalogue
structural, textual and dynamic techniques and note that they are usually evaluated in
isolation. Ko et al.~\cite{ko2006exploratory} observed developers navigating largely by
identifier names and search rather than by following dependencies.

\paragraph{Change history.} Zimmermann et al.~\cite{zimmermann2004mining} and Ying et
al.~\cite{ying2004predicting} mine co-change from version histories to suggest files that
change together. Our co-edited evidence source is the same notion of relatedness, used as
ground truth rather than as a method.

\paragraph{Graph-based context for agents.} SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} and its
successors~\cite{badertdinov2025swerebench,zhang2025swebenchlive} made repository-scale
change tasks a standard benchmark, and a family of systems now assembles context by walking
a code graph: Aider's repository map~\cite{aider2023repomap},
RepoGraph~\cite{ouyang2025repograph}, LocAgent~\cite{chen2025locagent} and
CoSIL~\cite{jiang2025cosil}. Agentless~\cite{xia2025agentless} is a notable counterexample that
leans on file and directory names.

What these systems share is the ground truth they are judged against.
Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys} records it for every system whose evaluation section we read in
the published PDF; each entry is quoted or paraphrased from that section, not from an
abstract or a secondary description.
Where localization accuracy is reported at all, the target is the set of files or functions
touched by the gold patch --- the SWE-bench convention, and exactly our \m{co\_edited}
source. That is the evidence source on which, in our results, structural proximity is the
weaker of the two signals on the uncontrolled comparison --- an ordering that the leakage
control of Section~\ref{sec:leak} then removes.

\paragraph{Leakage from the issue text.} That a benchmark's issue reports can contain their
own answers is known. SWE-Bench+~\cite{aleithan2024swebenchplus} finds that 32.67\% of the
patches SWE-Agent with GPT-4 gets \emph{passed} had the solution already present in the issue
report or its comments, and Agentless~\cite{xia2025agentless} reports a manual pass over
SWE-bench Lite that turns up problems whose issue description contains the exact ground-truth
patch. Both concern the \emph{solution}: the code, or a direct statement of the fix.

A weaker form concerns only \emph{where}. A retrieval component does not need the fix; it
needs only to know which files to open, and an issue that says \texttt{core.py} has supplied
that without supplying anything else. This too is known. The same Agentless study classifies
the location information in SWE-bench Lite's issues and finds that around half already
provide the location of the file to be edited; and the SWE-Bench Illusion
study~\cite{liang2025illusion} shows that models can name the buggy file from the issue alone,
without seeing the repository, in up to 76\% of SWE-bench Verified tasks against 53\% on
repositories outside SWE-bench. Our own rate, 40.2\% of tasks naming a key file as code and 12.6\% quoting a full
path, is in line with the first. What we add is not the rate but its consequence for
retrieval measurement: how much of an issue-aware method's score it accounts for, separated
within task from the rest of what the issue says (Section~\ref{sec:issue}). None of the
systems in Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys} reports its results by this stratum, and the practice we
argue for in Section~\ref{sec:leak} is to do so as routinely as reporting the corpus size.

\paragraph{Concurrent work is questioning the key.} The patch convention is under active
revision, by at least four efforts that appeared while this study was running.
SWE-Explore~\cite{zhang2026sweexplore} derives
line-level ground truth ``from independent agent trajectories that successfully solved the
same issue, distilling the specific code regions their solution paths actually consulted'',
and scores a ranked list ``under a fixed line budget'' --- both the key and the cost model
are close relatives of ours. ContextBench~\cite{li2026contextbench} annotates gold context
by hand, 522{,}115 lines over 1{,}136 tasks, and measures recall, precision and efficiency
rather than end-to-end resolution. AgentRetrievalBench~\cite{qin2026agentretrievalbench}
defines a file as relevant ``when reading it would materially help the agent take the next
correct step'', evaluated under a top-$k$ or token budget; one of its four task types,
ripple files beyond an anchored edit, is our co-edited source by another name. And
GraphLocator~\cite{liu2025graphlocator} keeps the patch key but dual-annotates it, on the
stated grounds that patch-derived ground truth misses locations.

We take this as corroboration of the premise rather than as a threat to it: several groups
independently concluded in the same year that the patch key is inadequate. What none of
them reports is the consequence we measure. Each proposes a better key and evaluates
methods against it; we hold two keys already recoverable from existing benchmark data, and
show that the choice between them changes the ranking of the methods themselves. The
contribution is not the observation that keys differ, and it is not the reversal either:
Sections~\ref{sec:shared} and~\ref{sec:leak} show that both halves of that reversal are
produced by confounds rather than by the signals. The contribution is the controls that
establish this, and the measurement in Section~\ref{sec:issue} of how little issue text adds
once the tasks whose issues name the answer are set aside.

\paragraph{Retrieval.} BM25~\cite{robertson2009bm25} remains the reference lexical ranking
function; we use it unchanged, varying only the query.

\section{Study Design}

\label{sec:design-freeze}
The corpus, the graph builder, the task definition and the coverage--cost metric were fixed
and tagged in version control before any method was run; the present study adds method
families and analyses on top of that frozen base. Changes made after that tag, and claims we
have retracted, are recorded in the replication package rather than silently absorbed.

The freeze covers the corpus, the graphs, the task definition and the metric. It does not
cover the method families: the fusion orderings, the directed walks and the lexical methods
queried by issue text were all added afterwards, in response to what the first results
showed. Fusion is the paper's main recommendation and it was an \emph{exploratory} result when
we first found it. We then tested it twice under predictions committed before any data were
scored: on seven repositories outside the sample (Section~\ref{sec:external}) and against a
human-annotated key (Section~\ref{sec:contextbench}). Three later additions, made in response
to review, were not fixed in advance and are reported as exploratory: the two alternative
cost rules (Section~\ref{sec:metric}), a dense retriever (Section~\ref{sec:dense}) and a
condition without a free seed (Section~\ref{sec:seedless}).

We also use ``design freeze'' rather than ``pre-registration'' throughout, and mean the
weaker thing. The freeze is a signed tag in our own version control, not a record lodged
with an external registry, so it establishes the order in which we did things to a reader
who trusts the repository and to nobody else. The protocol in
Section~\ref{sec:protocol} has the same status. We report it because stating a design before
running it is worth something even unregistered, not because it carries the guarantee that
an OSF entry would.

\subsection{Repositories and tasks}

\begin{sloppypar}
We searched SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live, SWE-Gym, SWE-bench Pro, Loc-Bench and SWE-rebench for
candidate repositories, and drew the sample's pull requests from three of them --- SWE-bench,
SWE-bench-Live and SWE-rebench --- keeping Python repositories that pass the sampling rules; the
repositories whose tasks come only from SWE-Gym or SWE-bench Pro form the external set of
Section~\ref{sec:external}. A pull request that
edits $k$ existing non-test source files that are nodes of the import graph yields $k$
tasks: each edited file in turn becomes the \emph{seed}, and the task is to order the
remaining files of the repository. This gives 3{,}123 tasks from 1{,}873 pull requests in
113 repositories. Of these, 2{,}412 tasks --- 1{,}162 pull requests in 112 repositories ---
have at least one key file inside the graph once the seed is removed, and they are the ones
scored here; the remaining 711 tasks have an empty key under both sources and are reported
but not scored. Those 711 tasks come from 711 distinct pull requests, and 706 of them change
a single file: with no second edited file there is no co-edited key, and the symbol key is
empty whenever the changed code resolves to nothing outside itself --- standard library,
third-party packages, or names \texttt{jedi} could not resolve. That is 61.2\% of all
single-file tasks, which is a real limitation of the symbol key and not a filtering choice
of ours. Within the scored set, 1{,}958 tasks (708 pull requests) have a co-edited
key and 2{,}341 (1{,}156 pull requests) a symbol key.
\end{sloppypar}

The median task's repository has 131 graph nodes, and the median key is 2 files under
either source --- 3 files totalling 1{,}515 lines if the two are pooled, as they are only in
Table~\ref{tab:distance} --- so the task is to find a handful of files among roughly a
hundred.

\subsection{Import graphs}

Graphs are built per base commit with a custom \m{ast} walker over the repository at that
commit. Nodes are source files; an edge $a \rightarrow b$ means $a$ imports a module
resolving to $b$. Package \m{\_\_init\_\_} files are not inserted as intermediaries,
\m{from X import Y} resolves to the module, edges are unweighted, imports inside
\m{TYPE\_CHECKING} blocks and inside function bodies are kept, and test files are excluded.
Per-file line counts come from the same pass and are the cost unit throughout.

\subsection{Two evidence sources}
\label{sec:keys}

\begin{description}
\item[\m{co\_edited}] The other non-test source files changed by the same pull request. This
is what a developer in fact touched, and it is independent of the import graph.
\item[\m{symbol}] Files that define names the changed code references, resolved with a static
analyser. This is what the change depends on.
\end{description}

\noindent Symbol resolution uses \texttt{jedi}'s \texttt{goto} with
\texttt{follow\_imports=True}, which reaches a name's defining file by traversing import
statements. This bounds what the symbol key can show: the key is constructed by walking the import graph, so a method that walks the import graph
is being scored against a target built from the same substrate. We report it because it is
the natural static notion of ``what this code depends on'', not because it is a neutral
arbiter between the two method families. Names are resolved in the code with the pull
request's patch applied, from the lines it adds, and a defining file must already exist at the
base commit. A definition the fix itself adds can therefore put a file in the symbol key, but
only a file the fix modifies, which is also in the co-edited key; 47.5\% of symbol-key file
references are, which bounds that effect from above.

\noindent By \emph{issue text} we mean the problem statement only; the \texttt{hints\_text}
some benchmarks ship, written after the fact by maintainers, is not used.

\noindent The seed file is removed from both. We deliberately do not merge them: the whole
question is whether the choice matters. It does, and the union is not a neutral compromise
--- the symbol key contributes 7{,}675 file references against 4{,}458 for co-editing, so a
union largely inherits the structural source's verdict.

A third source --- files actually executed by the tests that the fix repairs --- is defined
in our protocol and was collected for 113 pull requests before we stopped. We exclude it
rather than report it: a source covering under a tenth of the corpus cannot be compared
against two that cover all of it, and reporting it alongside them would invite exactly the
conflation this paper argues against. The partial collection is in the replication package
so that it is visible rather than quietly dropped, and completing it is the obvious
extension.

\subsection{Reading orders}

Every method receives the graph at the base commit, the seed file, per-file identifier bags
and the issue text, and returns an ordering of all other nodes. Table~\ref{tab:methods}
lists them by family. Identifier bags are built by splitting every identifier in the file on
underscores and camel-case boundaries and lower-casing; the issue text is tokenised
identically, so text is matched against code over one vocabulary. BM25 is used with the
standard $k_1 = 1.5$, $b = 0.75$ and differs between methods only in the query. Fusion is
reciprocal-rank fusion with $k = 60$.

Every issue-aware ordering in Table~\ref{tab:methods} is lexical. To test whether a learned
representation extracts more from an issue than BM25 does, we also score a dense retriever,
added after the main results (Section~\ref{sec:dense}). It uses the embedding model fixed in
our design before any method ran, \texttt{jina-embeddings-v2-base-code}, on the first 512
tokens of each file; an issue is embedded whole, as the length-weighted mean of its 512-token
chunks, so that nothing in it is truncated. Files are ranked by cosine similarity to the issue
(\m{dense\_issue}) or to the seed file (\m{dense\_seed}), and the dense ranking is fused with
the length-aware walk in place of BM25 over contents or beside it. These orderings are scored
but kept out of the ranks and correction families of the other tables, so that adding them
moves nothing reported elsewhere.

Two asymmetries matter. The structural methods are \emph{given} a correct
answer for free --- the seed is one of the files the pull request changed. The issue-text
methods are given no seed at all. And the metric charges by lines read, so we include
length-aware variants (suffix \m{\_pl}, score divided by file length) to separate ``ranks the
right files highly'' from ``happens to prefer short files''.

\caption{Reading orders, by family. Structural methods use the seed and the graph; global
methods use neither the seed nor the issue; lexical methods use no graph.}
\label{tab:methods}

\midrule
global & \m{pagerank} & PageRank of the whole graph; ignores seed and issue \\
 & \m{indegree} & number of files importing this one \\
\midrule
lexical & \m{bm25\_seed} & BM25, query = identifiers of the seed file \\
 & \m{path\_seed} & BM25 over paths, query = the seed's path tokens \\
 & \m{bm25\_issue} & BM25, query = identifiers of the issue text \\
 & \m{bm25\_issue\_pl} & the same, divided by file length \\
 & \m{path\_issue} & BM25 over file paths, query = issue tokens \\
\midrule
fusion & \m{rrf\_hops\_path} & RRF of \m{hops\_lines} and \m{path\_issue} \\
 & \m{rrf\_hops\_issue\_path} & RRF of \m{hops\_lines}, \m{bm25\_issue}, \m{path\_issue} \\
 & \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} & RRF of \m{ppr\_und\_pl}, \m{bm25\_issue}, \m{path\_issue} \\
 & \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue} & RRF of \m{ppr\_und} and \m{bm25\_issue} \\
 & \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue\_path} & RRF of \m{ppr\_und}, \m{bm25\_issue}, \m{path\_issue} \\
\midrule
reference & \m{same\_dir} & files in the seed's directory first \\
 & \m{random} & uniformly shuffled: the floor \\
 & \m{oracle} & key files only, cheapest first: the ceiling \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Metric}

An ordering is read from the top, whole file by whole file, until the next file would exceed
the line budget; reading stops there, so no file is skipped to fit a smaller one further down
and none is read in part. Coverage is the fraction of the key that has been read. We evaluate at budgets
$\{250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000\}$ and report the AUC, the mean coverage
over those eight doublings, so that a method must be good at both tight and generous
budgets. We also report the more directly interpretable quantity: the number of lines that
must be read before half the key has been covered.

Orderings with ties are re-drawn three times per task with distinct seeds and the coverage
curves averaged.

The upper budgets approach the whole repository for the smaller repositories, which could
compress differences between methods. Restricting the AUC to the six budgets up to 8{,}000
lines leaves the leading orderings unchanged under both keys and on both populations.

The budget is denominated in lines because the pre-registered design fixed it that way at
\texttt{freeze-1}, and we do not change a frozen metric after seeing results. Lines are
nevertheless the wrong unit for a context window, so we measure the conversion rather than
assume it: across the 121{,}075 distinct file versions in the corpus, tokenised with the
\texttt{cl100k\_base} byte-pair vocabulary, Python source runs to 8.50 tokens per line in
aggregate and a median of 7.88 per file, with a 5th--95th percentile range of 5.70--10.90.
Absolute counts shift by a small constant factor between tokenizer families; the ratios we
report do not depend on the choice. A budget of 8{,}000 lines is therefore roughly 68{,}000
tokens, and the eight budgets span roughly 2{,}100 to 272{,}000 tokens --- from a
fraction of a small context window to more than a large one.

\subsection{Statistics}
\label{sec:stats}

Task AUCs are averaged within a pull request first, so a change touching many files does not
count many times. Paired comparisons use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with the
Vargha--Delaney $A_{12}$ effect size, Holm-corrected within each family of comparisons.
Confidence intervals are 2{,}000-resample bootstraps resampling \emph{repositories}, not
tasks, so that a few large repositories cannot manufacture significance.

Every rank in this paper is on one scale: position among the twenty-three orderings we score,
the oracle included, so the best attainable non-oracle rank is 2. Where we say ``the twenty
contenders'' we mean the subset entered into the paired tests --- the twenty-three less the
oracle, \m{indegree} and \m{bfs\_und}, which are reported for reference but not tested. Two
further orderings, the issue-free fusion twins of Section~\ref{sec:issue}, are scored but
never ranked: they are controls rather than candidate reading orders, and ranking them would
shift every other rank in every table.

The paired tests are reported with the \textbf{repository} as the unit: the pull-request
scores are averaged within a repository and the test runs over the 112 repositories. Pull
requests are not independent draws --- they cluster in repositories that differ in size,
layout convention and issue-writing culture --- and a test that ignores the clustering
counts the same evidence many times. The difference is not cosmetic, though it does not
touch the headline comparisons, which are significant either way. It touches the borderline
ones: of the 1{,}076 paired comparisons on the two keys that are significant after Holm
correction with the pull request as the unit, 102 are not with the repository as the unit,
and 2 move the other way; no estimate changes sign. One of the 102 is a comparison this paper would otherwise have
leaned on --- \m{hops\_lines} against \m{path\_issue} on co-edited files, $p_{\text{Holm}} <
10^{-4}$ over pull requests and $0.07$ over repositories. We report the pull-request-level
tests alongside, in the replication package, so the two can be compared.

Averaging within a repository has a cost of its own: a repository that contributes one pull
request weighs as much as one that contributes a hundred. So every comparison a claim rests
on is also re-estimated as a linear mixed model of the per-pull-request paired difference,
with a random intercept per repository (Table~\ref{tab:mixed}). It keeps every pull request
as an observation and models the clustering instead of averaging it away. On 40 of those 41
comparisons it reaches the same verdict, significant or not, as the repository-level Wilcoxon
test. The exception is the borderline comparison above: weighting repositories by their pull
requests, the mixed model finds path matching better than \m{hops\_lines} on co-edited files
by 0.044 ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-3}$), where the repository-level test does not. We report
it, and no claim in this paper rests on that comparison being null.

Holm correction is applied within families that are fixed by the design rather than chosen
per claim. Table~\ref{tab:families} lists them: each set of paired tests for one key, one
unit, one population and one leakage stratum is one family of 325 tests, among twenty-six
orderings --- the twenty contenders, the two issue-free twins and the four names-redacted
variants of Section~\ref{sec:issue}, so that every twin and redaction comparison has its
test; each redaction arm is one family; and the mixed-model
re-estimates are one family.

Because a co-edited key requires a pull request that touches more than one graph file while
a symbol key does not, the two keys do not cover the same pull requests. Wherever we compare
across keys we therefore report the comparison twice: over each key's full population, and
over the 702 pull requests that carry both (Section~\ref{sec:shared}).

\section{Results}

\subsection{RQ1: the two-hop neighbourhood is half the repository}

``The files you need are within two hops'' is true here: 86.7\% of symbol-key files and
88.1\% of co-edited files lie within two undirected hops of the seed
(Table~\ref{tab:distance}). Taken alone this reads as strong evidence for graph retrieval.

The other half of the statistic undoes it. The median two-hop ball holds 68 files and
21{,}646 lines, more than five times a 4{,}000-line budget. Measured task by task against its
own repository, the ball is a median 58.5\% of it and a mean 55.6\%. Its median precision is
3.4\%. Against a random sample of the same size it lifts recall by a factor of 1.57.

The two-hop neighbourhood is therefore not a filter. It is a statement that the files you
need are somewhere in about half the repository --- which is exactly the regime in which the
\emph{ordering} decides everything and the graph has already said all it has to say.

\subsection{RQ2: the two keys rank the methods differently}

Table~\ref{tab:main} is the uncontrolled comparison, and the one whose reading the rest
of this section revises. Throughout the paper, the AUC in a table is a mean over pull
requests, while a difference quoted in the text is the mean of the paired
per-repository differences, because the repository is the unit every test uses
(Section~\ref{sec:stats}). The two agree to within a few thousandths and can differ in the
third decimal. Under the co-edited key the five best non-oracle orderings
are four fusions and one lexical method; the best purely structural ordering is tenth, and
the query-independent priors are twenty-first and twenty-second of twenty-three, below
\m{same\_dir} and barely above random. Under the symbol key the table inverts: the four best
non-oracle orderings are three structural orderings and one fusion, and the best lexical ordering is fifteenth.

The individual reversals are large and significant after Holm correction with the repository
as the unit. Issue-text path matching beats length-aware personalised PageRank by 0.059 AUC
on co-edited files ($A_{12} = 0.403$ for the walk, $p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$) and loses to
it by 0.100 on symbol files ($A_{12} = 0.671$, $p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-7}$).

We rest the reversal on those paired tests rather than on a rank correlation. The
correlation is low --- Spearman $\rho = 0.24$ over the twenty contenders ($p = 0.31$), and
$\rho = 0.37$ over all twenty-two non-oracle orderings ($p = 0.09$) --- but with twenty
points a non-significant $\rho$ is weak evidence of anything, and its value moves with which
methods are included. The Holm-corrected pairwise reversals do not have that weakness.

Two things about Table~\ref{tab:main} are \emph{not} safe to read off it, and the next two
subsections are about them. The two columns are computed over different pull requests, and
the left column is computed over a corpus in which many issues name the answer outright.
Each of those turns out to account for one of the two halves of the reversal.

Figure~\ref{fig:curves} shows the same reversal as coverage curves. Table~\ref{tab:lines}
states it in the unit a context budget is actually spent in: to reach half the co-edited
files a reader following length-aware personalised PageRank consumes a median of 6{,}155
lines, against 4{,}838 following issue-text path matching and 3{,}342 following the best
fusion. On symbol files the same three numbers are 3{,}483, 6{,}638 and 3{,}957 --- the walk
and the words trade places, and the fusion is close to the better of the two in both.

\subsection{The reversal is smaller on a matched population}
\label{sec:shared}

A co-edited key exists only for a pull request that changes more than one file in the graph.
A symbol key does not need that, and 454 of the 1{,}156 pull requests with a symbol key
change a single file. The two columns of Table~\ref{tab:main} are therefore scored on
different samples, and single-file changes are exactly the case where a seed's import
neighbourhood is most of what there is to find. The comparison has to be repeated on a
population that carries both keys.

Table~\ref{tab:shared} does that, on the 702 pull requests that have both. On the co-edited
key nothing moves: no method changes rank by more than one place. On the symbol key the
structural family loses most of its advantage. Cost-scaled personalised PageRank along
import edges falls from second to eighth (0.491 to 0.417), the undirected form from third to
fifth, and \m{hops\_lines} from fourth to sixth, while issue-to-path matching rises from
fifteenth to ninth. The three top places under both keys are then held by the same three
fusions.

The statistical claim moves with the ranks. On the full corpus a walk along import edges
beats path matching on the symbol key by 0.101 ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-7}$, repository as
the unit). On the matched population the same comparison gives $+0.008$ and
$p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$; for \m{hops\_lines} against path matching it gives $+0.019$ and
$p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$. We therefore do not claim that structural proximity beats issue-text
retrieval on the symbol key. On a like-for-like sample the two are indistinguishable, and
what remains of the reversal is the co-edited half --- which the next control also qualifies.

\subsection{Direction: reversing a walk is costly, discarding it is free}
\label{sec:direction}

The walks above are undirected, as they are in most of this literature. An import edge has a
direction, so we add both orientations of the personalised walk, length-aware and not.

The result is asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the finding. Running the walk \emph{along}
import edges --- towards what the seed depends on --- places \m{ppr\_out\_pl} second of
twenty-three on the symbol key at 0.491. Running it \emph{against} them collapses to
\m{ppr\_in\_pl} at 0.277, twenty-first. The like-for-like gap is 0.123 on the matched
population and 0.215 on the full one ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-14}$, repository as the
unit), and on the symbol key the ten largest gaps between any two structural orderings, on
either population, all have an inward walk on the losing side.

But the undirected walk loses almost nothing. On the symbol key \m{ppr\_und\_pl} scores
0.489 against \m{ppr\_out\_pl}'s 0.491, a paired difference of 0.001 that is not significant
on the full corpus ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$) and reverses in sign on the matched one, where the
undirected walk leads by 0.020 ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.85$). So
the practice this literature has settled on --- throw the direction away --- is not the
mistake it might appear to be from the spread of the table. Walking backwards is the mistake.

On the co-edited key direction is worse than useless. All four directed variants rank
seventeenth to twentieth, below \m{same\_dir}, a baseline that orders files by directory and
consults no graph at all; all four undirected walks rank tenth to fourteenth, above it.
Committing to an orientation costs 0.040 to 0.064 AUC there ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-3}$).

The explanation is the same one that qualifies the symbol key throughout. That key is built
by resolving names with \texttt{jedi}, which follows imports in exactly one direction, so a
walk in that direction is measuring something close to the key's own construction. The
co-edited key records a human decision about what belonged in one change, and no orientation
of the import graph recovers it well.

\subsection{RQ3: what the seed is worth depends on the source too}

A query-independent PageRank prior --- a ranking that never looks at the seed or the issue,
and simply says which files matter in this repository --- reaches 0.410 on symbol files
against 0.491 for the best length-aware personalised walk, which does look at the seed. That
is 83\% of the personalised score in absolute terms, or 67\% of its margin over a random
ordering, which is the fairer of the two readings and the one the fourth recommendation in
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} quotes. It
is far above random (0.248; $A_{12} = 0.758$,
$p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-16}$). On that evidence source, much of what the personalised walk
delivers is a repository prior.

Under the co-edited key the same prior scores 0.271 against a random floor of 0.248. The
difference is significant but negligible ($A_{12} = 0.552$, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.002$), and
the personalised walk beats it by 0.101 ($A_{12} = 0.666$). Knowing which file is being changed therefore
matters a great deal for predicting what else was changed, and rather little for predicting
what the code calls, where knowing the repository's hubs is nearly as good.

The opposite claim is easy to make from a single source: whether ``the graph knows what you are working on'' appears true or false is itself
a function of the answer key.

\subsection{RQ4: the two signals name different files}
\label{sec:rq4}

The reversal is not two methods disagreeing about the order of one list. At $k=10$ the
top-10 sets of personalised PageRank and issue-text BM25 have a mean Jaccard overlap of
0.187, and of personalised PageRank and issue-text path matching only 0.102; at $k=50$ these
rise to 0.508 and 0.412. For comparison, personalised PageRank and the query-independent
prior overlap at 0.364 at $k=10$: a seed-conditioned walk resembles the repository prior
more than it resembles a lexical ranking.

Table~\ref{tab:comp} follows individual key files. At $k=20$, 24.4\% of co-edited files are
found only by the lexical family and 9.5\% only by the structural family; on symbol files the
asymmetry flips (20.0\% structure-only against 16.5\% words-only). Under either source about
a sixth of key files are found by neither family at $k=20$, which is where the remaining
headroom to the oracle lives.

\subsection{RQ5: fusion is the only ordering that survives both sources}
\label{sec:fusion}

If the evidence source is not known in advance --- and for a tool shipped to users it is not
--- the quantity to optimise is the worst a method does across sources. We report that two
ways. Worst-case \emph{rank} is easy to read but depends on the competitor set: adding our
four directed walks reshuffled everything below them, and a criterion that moves when other
people's methods are added is a poor one to recommend. Worst-case \emph{shortfall} --- the
largest AUC gap to the best non-oracle ordering under either key --- says the same thing in
units nobody else's entries can change. Table~\ref{tab:worst} gives both and sorts by the
second. The two agree on the family and disagree on its best member:
\m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} has the smaller shortfall (0.017 against 0.029) while
\m{rrf\_hops\_path} has the better worst rank (5 against 6). We recommend the former, because
the shortfall criterion, the matched population (Section~\ref{sec:shared}) and the held-out
splits (Section~\ref{sec:heldout}) all select it and only the rank criterion does not. Three of the five fusions beat every pure signal. The
two that do not --- \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue} and \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue\_path} --- are not
distinguished by whether they include path matching, since four of the five do and one
of those still fails. They are the two built on the unscaled \m{ppr\_und}. The three that
survive all fuse from a \emph{length-aware} structural input: either \m{ppr\_und\_pl}, whose
scores are divided by file length, or \m{hops\_lines}, which breaks ties between equidistant
files by preferring the shorter one. The two differ in how they use length and agree in that
they use it at all.

One pair isolates that property exactly. \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} and
\m{rrf\_ppr\_issue\_path} fuse the same three lists and differ only in whether the walk's
scores are divided by file length first; their worst-case ranks are 6 and 11, and the
difference is $+0.042$ AUC on co-edited files and $+0.050$ on symbol files on the matched
population ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-11}$, repository as the unit). \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue}
differs from its length-aware counterpart in two ways at once, so we rest the claim on the
clean pair rather than on the three-of-five tally. How much of this margin the cost rule
itself creates is the subject of Section~\ref{sec:metric}.

The insurance is close to free. Over the full corpus \m{rrf\_hops\_path} gains 0.067 AUC on
\m{hops\_lines} on co-edited files ($A_{12} = 0.602$, $p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-11}$) and is
indistinguishable from it on symbol files ($+0.003$ as a mean of repository differences,
$-0.001$ in the pull-request means of Table~\ref{tab:main}; $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$); against \m{ppr\_und\_pl} it gains 0.087
($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-13}$) and loses 0.008 ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$). The lexical signal
adds a large amount where structure is weak and costs nothing where structure is strong.
Section~\ref{sec:issue} asks what, in that lexical signal, is doing the work.

\subsection{How much of the ranking is the cost rule?}
\label{sec:metric}

The frozen metric charges whole files by their lines and stops at the first file that would
overflow the budget. Under that rule, dividing a score by file length is close to a knapsack
heuristic for the metric itself, and a long file placed early costs twice: its own lines, and
every later file that no longer fits. The length-awareness result could therefore belong to
the rule rather than to the signals. We rescored every ordering under two other rules, neither
fixed in advance. Under \emph{skip}, a file that does not fit is passed over and reading
continues, so an early long file costs only its own lines. Under \emph{files}, every file
costs one unit whatever its length, at budgets of 1 to 128 files --- the accounting of an
agent whose cost is the number of files it opens rather than their size.
Table~\ref{tab:metric} gives the leading orderings under all three rules.

Under the skip rule the recommendation stands. The fusion is the best non-oracle ordering on
the symbol key and 0.002 behind \m{rrf\_hops\_issue\_path} on the co-edited key; over the
full corpus it is 0.003 behind on the co-edited key and leads on the symbol key, where under
the frozen rule the walks lead. But the margin that
length-awareness buys shrinks by about sixty per cent: the clean pair of
Section~\ref{sec:fusion} separates by $+0.015$ and $+0.021$ instead of $+0.042$ and $+0.050$,
still significant ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$), and for the walks alone dividing by length
no longer helps at all (\m{ppr\_und\_pl} minus \m{ppr\_und} is $-0.018$ on co-edited files).
Under the per-file rule length-awareness is a cost everywhere, as it must be when a short
file buys nothing: the length-aware fusion falls to seventh and fifth, 0.055 and 0.045 behind
its unscaled twin \m{rrf\_ppr\_issue\_path}, which becomes the best ordering under both keys.

What survives every rule is the fusion of structure with issue text: on the matched
population, under each rule and on each key, a fusion is the best non-oracle ordering, and
under two of the three rules a length-aware fusion is. Which structural input to fuse depends on how reading is paid for. Where a context
is charged by size, as a token window is, make the walk length-aware; where it is charged by
the number of files opened, do not. We state contribution~2 accordingly.

\subsection{The fusion holds on repositories it was not chosen on}
\label{sec:heldout}

Both the fusion recipe and the worst-rank criterion that selects it were settled after we had
seen the full results. That makes the recommendation exploratory however large its margin, so
we split the corpus. A random 56 of the 112 repositories form a selection half; the
remaining 56 are set aside. We apply the criterion mechanically to the selection half ---
among the fusions, take the one whose worst rank across the two keys is best --- and then
report that ordering, unexamined, on the other half. Both halves are scored on the matched
population of Section~\ref{sec:shared}, the pull requests carrying both keys, because that is
the population on which a comparison across keys means anything; this is why the criterion
picks \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} here although on the unmatched Table~\ref{tab:worst} the
same criterion prefers \m{rrf\_hops\_path}. Splitting by repository rather than by
pull request keeps every task of a repository on one side, which is what the clustering in
Section~\ref{sec:stats} requires.

\begin{sloppypar}
One split would not settle much: with five candidates and a winner that is already best
overall, a single draw is close to a foregone conclusion. So we repeat it 200 times
(Table~\ref{tab:heldout}). \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} is selected in 198 of the 200 splits,
and in 195 of those it is the best non-oracle ordering on the co-edited key of the half that
did not select it, 198 of 198 on the symbol key. Its mean shortfall behind the best held-out
ordering is 0.002 AUC on co-edited files and 0.000 on symbol files. The two splits that
select \m{rrf\_hops\_issue\_path} instead do not confirm it.
\end{sloppypar}

What this establishes should not be overstated. The 200 splits are resamples of the same 112
repositories, and the selected fusion is already the best overall on the matched population,
so agreement across them is largely expected: they show that the choice is \emph{stable} ---
no small group of repositories is carrying it --- not that it generalises to repositories we
did not sample. Section~\ref{sec:external} tests that on repositories outside the sample. Nor
does it make the fusion family a discovery; it was chosen by us, from five candidates, on these
data.

\m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} is also insensitive to the one free parameter we chose without
testing. Reciprocal-rank fusion's $k$ was fixed at the customary 60; re-running the whole
pipeline at $k = 10$ and $k = 200$ moves its AUC by at most 0.007 on the co-edited key and
0.010 on the symbol key, an order of magnitude below the differences this section turns on.

\subsection{An external test on seven repositories the study never saw}
\label{sec:external}

Seven repositories pass every one of our sampling rules and were left out only because we
restricted the task sources to SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live and SWE-rebench: ansible, hydra,
moto, modin, MONAI, pydantic and qutebrowser, whose eligible tasks come from SWE-Gym and
SWE-bench Pro. We drew their tasks by the main sample's rule, seed and cap --- 140 pull
requests --- and then, \emph{before building a graph, a key or a score for any of them},
committed four predictions with their failure criteria to the replication package
(\texttt{paper/external\_prereg.md}); the version history records the order. The pipeline
then ran unchanged. Of the 140 pull requests, 139 yield a task and 96 have a non-empty key
under at least one source, 66 under both. Seven repositories are too few for the
repository-level Wilcoxon test --- its smallest two-sided $p$ at $n = 7$ is 0.016 --- so the
predictions name the mixed model of Section~\ref{sec:stats} as their test, with the caveat,
stated in advance, that seven groups estimate the random intercept poorly. These repositories
are also larger than the sample's (a median of 289 non-test Python files against 160), and
two of them are copyleft.

Table~\ref{tab:external} gives the four outcomes. Three predictions hold. The recommended
fusion is third on the oracle-inclusive scale under both keys, second only to
\m{rrf\_hops\_issue\_path}, a fusion of the same family, and its worst shortfall is 0.030 ---
at the limit we set, not inside it. It is never significantly worse than a pure ordering, and
walking inward is as costly as in the main sample. In these larger repositories the path-matching
fusions take ranks two to five under \emph{both} keys; on the symbol key the length-aware
walks no longer lead, as they do on the main sample's single-file changes.

The fourth fails. Deleting the key files' names from issues that name them costs the fusion
0.033 on the symbol key, significantly, but 0.030 on the co-edited key with $p_{\text{Holm}}
= 0.11$, on only 33 matched pull requests in six repositories; the control part --- the
redaction moves nothing where nothing is named --- holds. So the causal effect of the names
alone is not established on the co-edited key here, and where it is measured it is half the
size it is in the main sample. The wider arms, which we did not predict, cost the fusion
0.086 and 0.090 on the co-edited key: in these repositories an issue points at its files
through their directories far more than through their names, which is what one would expect of
code bases whose modules are named for deep package paths. The share of issues naming a key
file as code, 40.6\%, is the main sample's to within half a point.

\subsection{A human-annotated key}
\label{sec:contextbench}

Both of our keys are proxies, and the symbol key is built along the same import edges the
structural orderings walk. ContextBench~\cite{li2026contextbench} annotates by hand the code
an agent must see to reconstruct a passing fix. Its 409 Python tasks from SWE-bench Verified
and SWE-bench Pro come from datasets we already hold, so we ran them through the unchanged
pipeline with a third key, \m{gold}: the Python files in a task's annotated context, less the
seed, restricted to graph nodes like the others. We drew the tasks by the main sample's
eligibility rule, seed and cap --- 203 pull requests in 15 repositories, ten of which are in
the main sample, as are 24 of the pull requests --- and committed four predictions before
building any graph or score (\texttt{paper/contextbench\_prereg.md}). This is a test of the
keys, not of generalisation to new code. Of the resulting tasks, 215 from 108 pull requests in
14 repositories have a non-empty gold key. A gold key has a median of 3 files; 59\% of its
files are also co-edited files and 63\% are also symbol files.

All four predictions hold (Table~\ref{tab:cbpred}). The fusion is the second-best non-oracle
ordering on the human key, 0.009 behind \m{rrf\_hops\_issue\_path}; it beats each of the four
pure orderings we named by 0.086 to 0.128 ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le 0.008$); walking outward
beats walking inward by 0.083; and the ranking of all twenty-two orderings under each proxy key
agrees with the ranking under the human key (Kendall $\tau = 0.59$ for the symbol key, 0.97 for
the co-edited key).

The more informative result is one we did not predict: \emph{the human key sides with the
co-edited key} (Table~\ref{tab:cbauc}). Under it the lexical and fused orderings rank as they
do under the co-edited key, while the length-aware walks, second and fifth under the symbol
key on these same tasks, fall to eleventh and fifteenth. The symbol key's preference for
structure is not corroborated by people's judgement of what had to be read. That is what the
circularity of its construction predicts, and it means the structural wins on the symbol key
in this paper are statements about that key. An objection is that the gold key contains the
edited files and agrees with the co-edited key by construction. So we also scored, as an
exploratory analysis added after the predictions were tested, the gold files that the fix
\emph{reads but does not edit} --- the context a graph walk is supposed to be best at
finding --- on the 85 pull requests that have any. There the walks and the issue-only
retrievers are indistinguishable (differences of 0.006 to 0.012, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$), and
the fusion leads: it beats the issue-only orderings by 0.082 and 0.084 ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le
0.008$) and the walks by 0.074 to 0.090, which at this size does not survive correction
($p_{\text{Holm}} \ge 0.12$).

The set is small --- 108 pull requests in 14 repositories --- and its annotators saw the fix,
so their notion of necessary context is itself a reconstruction. It is nonetheless the only
key in this paper that no part of our pipeline built, and the recommendation holds on it.

\subsection{RQ6: what a budget rules out, and what it does not}
\label{sec:ceiling}

A coverage number says how much of the key a method found. It does not say whether finding
all of it was possible. If the needed files together exceed the budget, no ordering of them
fits and no downstream system can succeed, however capable: a model cannot use a file it was
never given. That bound is a property of the task and the budget alone, so it can be
measured once and applied to every method at once --- and, usefully here, without running a
model.

Table~\ref{tab:ceiling} reports it. The complete answer fits a 32{,}000-token budget for
90.3\% of pull requests under the co-edited key and 87.3\% under the symbol key, and a
64{,}000-token budget for over 95\% of both. The task is not, in general, impossible at
realistic budgets.

\begin{table}
\caption{Share of pull requests whose \emph{entire} key fits within a token budget. This is
a ceiling: no ordering can exceed it, and no agent can act on files outside it.}
\label{tab:ceiling}
\small
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
Token budget & co\_edited (\%) & symbol (\%) \\
\midrule
\rows{tab_ceiling}
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:full} applies the same all-or-nothing criterion to the orderings, in the
frozen unit of lines: the share of pull requests each one takes to \emph{complete} coverage
within 8{,}000 lines. The oracle succeeds on 97.5\%. The best ordering on the co-edited key,
\m{rrf\_hops\_issue\_path}, completes 58.5\% of pull requests, and the best on the symbol key,
\m{hops\_lines}, 51.0\%.

The oracle reads only key files, so its success is partly definitional: fitting a small key
into a large budget is close to arithmetic. We therefore do not read the forty-point gap as
headroom that better ordering could be expected to recover; it is an upper bound on what
better selection could add, not an estimate. What the comparison does establish is the
converse. At 8{,}000 lines the budget is almost never the binding constraint, so an ordering
that fails to cover the key fails because of the order, not the budget --- which rules out
the explanation a reader is likely to reach for first.

Two medians in this paper look as though they disagree and do not. The median \emph{task}
needs 1{,}150 lines read before the co-edited key is fully covered (Table~\ref{tab:lines}),
while Table~\ref{tab:ceiling} says 54.2\% of \emph{pull requests} fit inside 8{,}000 tokens.
Averaging a pull request's tasks first gives a median of 991 lines, and at the median 7.88
tokens per line that is about 7{,}800 tokens --- just inside the budget, which is why just
over half of them fit.

The reversal of Table~\ref{tab:main} survives this stricter criterion:
\m{bm25\_issue} loses 14.9 points and \m{path\_issue} 11.5 points moving from the co-edited
key to the symbol key, while the outward walks gain the most (\m{ppr\_out} 15.2 points,
\m{ppr\_out\_pl} 14.7) and \m{pagerank} gains 11.5. The gain is not a property of
the structural family as such: the two inward walks lose 11.2 and 11.7 points, about as much
as \m{path\_issue}'s 11.5 and in the same direction. It is a property of walking the
direction the key was built along, not of using the graph.
And the fusion orderings again sit at or near the top of both columns, which is the same
conclusion RQ5 reached by AUC, reached here by a measure that ignores partial credit
entirely.

\subsection{Do the lexical methods just copy paths out of the issue?}
\label{sec:leak}

Issue reports often contain stack traces, and a stack trace names files. If the lexical
advantage came from reports quoting the paths of the files that had to change, a benchmark
average would describe issues that name their files, not issues in general --- which is the
sense in which we call it leakage. For a deployed tool the names are a legitimate input.

Much of the advantage does come from such issues, and the effect is big enough that we report
it as a result rather than as a reassurance.

The full path of a key file appears verbatim in the issue text for 12.6\% of tasks, and a
bare file stem for 48.5\%. Path BM25 tokenises a path into lowercased subtokens, so a stem is
enough to match and the full-path control is far too weak. But a bare stem is also too
strong a criterion on its own: an issue about ``models'' and a key file called
\texttt{models.py} share a word because a project's prose and its filenames draw on one
domain vocabulary, and using that overlap is retrieval, not leakage. We therefore classify
every stem occurrence by how it is written. A mention is \emph{explicit} if it appears as
code --- \texttt{core.py}, \texttt{simbad/core}, a dotted module path, inside backticks, or
inside a fenced or indented block --- and \emph{incidental} if the stem occurs only as an
ordinary English word. Explicit mentions cover 40.2\% of tasks. A further 8.3\% have
incidental matches only, the two together making up the 48.5\% of tasks with any stem at all.

That gives three nested strata: issues quoting no full key path (2{,}108 tasks), issues
naming no key file as code (1{,}442 tasks), and the strictest set containing no key stem at
all (1{,}243 tasks). We treat the middle one as primary. It removes the leakage channel while
leaving the vocabulary signal in place, and it does not select as heavily for vague issues as
the strictest does.

Table~\ref{tab:leak} applies this control \emph{together with} the population control of
Section~\ref{sec:shared}, recomputing within each stratum the set of pull requests that carry
both keys. Applied on its own, the leakage control would leave the symbol columns full of the
single-file pull requests that the matching control exists to remove, and a claim that
survives each control separately need not survive both. Reading the strata jointly is the
only version of this table we regard as evidence.

\paragraph{On co-edited files, path matching falls and structure does not follow it down.}
On the full corpus \m{path\_issue} is sixth of the twenty-three orderings. Under the weak
full-path control it barely moves, falling from 0.434 to 0.408 and holding sixth. Under the
primary control it falls to 0.363 and \emph{thirteenth}; under the strictest, to 0.339 and
fourteenth. \m{hops\_lines} --- pure structure, no issue text --- rises from tenth to sixth in
both. Because the middle and the strictest strata agree, the finding is not an artefact of
over-correcting: it does not depend on discarding incidental vocabulary overlap.

The direction of that change is clear; its significance is weaker than the ranks suggest, and
we report the tests rather than the gap. \m{hops\_lines} over \m{path\_issue} on co-edited
files is $-0.007$ under the full-path control ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$), $+0.042$ under the
primary control ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.60$) and $+0.056$ under the strictest
($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.04$). Only in the strictest stratum does pure structure beat path
matching outright. In the primary stratum the two become
\emph{indistinguishable}, which is already the interesting claim: the ordering that appeared
to be the best single signal on this key stops being distinguishable from one that never
reads the issue, once the issues that name the answer are removed. These strata are smaller
than the corpus --- 531 pull requests across 109 repositories in the primary stratum --- so
the failure to separate them is in part a matter of power, and we do not read it as evidence
of equivalence.

\paragraph{On symbol files, length-aware walks lead in the two stricter strata.} Under the
full-path control the fusion still leads (0.456, against 0.440 for \m{ppr\_und\_pl}). Under the
primary control and the strictest, \m{ppr\_und\_pl} and \m{hops\_lines} lead instead, second
and third on the oracle-inclusive scale in the primary stratum, at 0.445 and 0.435, with the best fusion fourth at 0.430. The gap is not significant ($+0.017$ for \m{ppr\_und\_pl},
$p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$), so this is a place where the fusion stops leading rather than a place
where it loses.

\paragraph{The seed is not the explanation.} The \m{path\_seed} control separates ``issue
text'' from ``path matching'' directly: the same path-BM25 ranking, queried by the seed's own
path instead of the issue, scores 0.371 on co-edited files against 0.434 for the issue query
($+0.058$, $p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$, repository as the unit), and the two are
indistinguishable on symbol files ($+0.020$, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.81$). For comparison, the issue names the
seed file --- the file every structural method is handed for free --- less often than it names
a key file: its full path appears in 10.3\% of tasks and its stem in 35.1\%, against 12.6\%
and 48.5\% for the key files.

\subsection{RQ7: what does reading the issue actually add?}
\label{sec:issue}

The previous subsection removes tasks. That answers whether a ranking survives the removal,
but it cannot say what the issue text contributes, for two reasons. Every ordering is
affected by which tasks are dropped; and the tasks that are dropped are not a random sample
of issues. A report containing a stack trace is plausibly longer, more technical and more
tractable than a one-line feature request, so a comparison across leakage strata compares
kinds of issue as well as degrees of leakage. We answer the question twice, once in each
direction, and the two answers together decompose the effect.

\paragraph{Across tasks: an issue-free twin.} For each of our two leading fusions we
construct a twin in which every issue-derived input is replaced by its seed-derived
counterpart. \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path}, which fuses a length-aware walk with BM25 over file
contents and BM25 over file paths, both queried by the issue, is paired with
\m{rrf\_pprpl\_seedpath}, which fuses the same walk with the same two BM25 rankings queried
by the \emph{seed file's own path and contents}. The twin sees the same graph, blends the
same number of lists through the same rank fusion, and runs the same retrieval machinery. It
simply never reads the issue. The difference is what the issue is worth, net of the ``a
fusion just gets more input'' explanation the fusion result otherwise invites.

Over the corpus the issue is worth $+0.069$ AUC on the co-edited key and $+0.055$ on the
symbol key, both strongly significant (Table~\ref{tab:issue}). Split by the leakage
classification, that becomes $+0.156$ and $+0.121$ on the 40.2\% of tasks whose issue names a
key file as code, against $+0.016$ and $+0.012$ on the rest, where neither survives
correction; requiring the stem to be absent as well takes it to $+0.003$ and $-0.002$. The
progression is monotone across five strata and holds for both pairs and both keys.

Because these are null results we report what they exclude rather than treating them as
zeros. The bootstrap interval on the no-mention stratum is $[0.000, 0.031]$ on the co-edited
key and $[-0.003, 0.027]$ on the symbol key, so the data are consistent with the issue being
worth up to about 0.03 AUC there, and inconsistent with its being worth anything close to the
0.156 it is worth where it names a file. Taken alone this comparison would say that the issue
is worth almost exactly what it names --- and taken alone it would be overstating, because it
is confounded with which issues, and which tasks, name their files.

\paragraph{Within task: redaction.} So we did the other experiment. For every task we take
the \emph{same} issue and delete only the occurrences of its key files' names that our
classifier calls explicit, leaving the prose, the traceback, the surrounding directory names
and the length untouched. Scoring the same task on both versions isolates the names
themselves: the issue, the writer, the project and the difficulty are all held fixed.

\begin{sloppypar}
What counts as ``the names'' is a choice, so we make it three times. The \emph{names} arm
removes only the stem and any immediately following \texttt{.py}: \texttt{astroquery/simbad/core.py}
becomes \texttt{astroquery/simbad/}. That leaves a channel open, since path BM25 tokenises
paths and the surviving directory names still point at the file, so the \emph{paths} arm also
deletes every component of each key file's path wherever it is written as code. Neither
touches a traceback's \texttt{in query\_object} or a backticked \texttt{Simbad.query\_object},
which a content ranking can match against the file that defines it, so the \emph{symbols} arm
also deletes every function, class and method name defined in a key file, again only where
written as code. The names arm is a lower bound on leakage. The wider arms over-remove ---
a directory called \texttt{models} or a method the user calls by name is also ordinary
vocabulary --- so the three bracket the effect rather than measure it.
\end{sloppypar}

The result is in Table~\ref{tab:redact}. Of the 970 tasks whose issues name a key file, the
848 in the matched population --- 378 pull requests in 105 repositories --- are scored; on
them, removing just the names costs \m{path\_issue} 0.110 AUC on the co-edited key and 0.092
on the symbol key, and the best fusion 0.061 and 0.050. Every one of these survives Holm
correction with the repository as the unit, and the bootstrap intervals are narrow: for
\m{path\_issue} on co-edited files it is $[0.090, 0.131]$, and the widest of the eight spans
0.041. The wider arms cost more, as they must: 0.148 and 0.157 for \m{path\_issue} on
co-edited files, 0.084 and 0.096 for the fusion. On the 1{,}072 matched tasks (531 pull
requests) among the 1{,}442 where the names arm found nothing to remove, it changes nothing
--- at most 0.002 in every cell, significant in none, which is the sanity check the design
demands. The wider arms do find something there, and cost the fusion 0.016 to 0.018: an issue
that never names a key file can still quote its directory or a function it defines.

\paragraph{The decomposition.} Both experiments run on the same matched population with the
repository as the unit, so their answers add up, and together they say something neither says
alone. On the tasks whose issue names a key file, the issue as a whole is worth $+0.156$ AUC
to the best fusion on the co-edited key and $+0.121$ on the symbol key. Of that, the names
account for $+0.061$ and $+0.050$, and the rest of the issue for $+0.095$ and $+0.071$, every
term significant under Holm correction. On the tasks whose issue names nothing, the issue as a
whole is worth $+0.016$ and $+0.012$, and neither is significant.

So both effects are real and neither subsumes the other. Filename leakage is causal and large:
path matching loses a fifth of its score on the affected tasks when only the names go, and
nearly three tenths under the widest arm. A reader of the stratified table alone would put
the whole $+0.140$ stratum difference down to leakage. Under the names arm $+0.061$ of it is
leakage and $+0.079$ is not; under the widest arm, taking into account that it also removes
something from issues that name nothing, the split is $+0.078$ and $+0.062$ (on the symbol key,
$+0.050$ to $+0.065$ of a $+0.109$ gap). What remains after every redaction we can define is
not leakage we can find, and we do not claim it is issue \emph{quality} either: it is a
difference between the issues that name files and the ones that do not, and between the
tasks they describe, that the redaction cannot reach. Even \m{path\_issue}, which reads
nothing but file paths, still scores 0.393 on the named-file tasks after the widest
redaction against 0.333 on the others after the same treatment, so some of that difference
is in what the issues say or in which files the tasks need, not in how the issues are
written.

\paragraph{What this licenses.} It does not show that issue text is useless for code
retrieval; developers use it, and an ordering that exploits a real report naming a
real file exploits something that exists. What it shows is that a benchmark assembled from
issue reports of this kind measures two things at once, and that the two can be bracketed for
the cost of a few regular expressions. Any evaluation on SWE-bench-derived data that reports a gain
from issue-aware retrieval and does not stratify is reporting their sum. That, rather than
the ranking of our own methods, is the finding we would most like the field to take up.

\subsection{Without a free seed}
\label{sec:seedless}

Every task so far hands the orderings the file being changed. An agent is not handed it: it
must find that file from the issue, and localisation is where agents are known to struggle. To
see whether the recommendation depends on the free seed, we removed it. For each of the
1{,}162 pull requests the issue alone picks a starting file --- the top of the reciprocal-rank
fusion of BM25 over contents and BM25 over paths, the two issue-only rankings used throughout
--- and every seed-conditioned ordering walks from that guess and reads it first. Issue-only
orderings need no seed and run unchanged over the whole repository. The unit is the pull
request, and the two keys become every existing source file it edits, the true seeds
included, so that finding the file to change is part of what is scored; and every file
defining a name the change uses. This analysis was added in response to review and is
exploratory.

The guess is right in 41\% of pull requests: in 53\% of the 583 whose issue names an edited
file as code, and in 29\% of the 579 whose issue does not. (Half the pull requests, not two
fifths of the tasks, count as naming here, because the seed's own name now counts.)

Table~\ref{tab:seedless} gives the result. Walking from the guess and fusing with the issue
remains the best non-oracle ordering under both keys, at 0.480 and 0.440, and in no stratum
is it significantly worse than any alternative. What the walk adds depends on the key. On the
symbol key it adds 0.044 to the issue-only fusion that chose its seed ($p_{\text{Holm}} <
10^{-4}$), and does so whether or not the issue names a file: even a wrong guess is usually in
the right package, and the walk reaches what the change depends on from there. On the edited
files it adds 0.009 ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.03$) and nothing significant within either stratum:
when the task is to find the files to change, what the issue retrieves directly is nearly all
there is. The walks on their own, without the issue, fall well behind on the edited files
(0.404 against 0.480), because the file they start from is wrong more often than right.

This is the simplest possible localiser, and an agent's is better; the numbers bound what a
graph adds on top of a weak guess, not a strong one. But the recommendation does not depend on
the free seed.

\subsection{Sensitivity: does the uncontrolled ranking survive in large repositories?}
\label{sec:size}

The corpus skews small --- the median repository contributes 131 graph nodes --- so the
reversal has to be shown not to be an artefact of repositories one can almost read whole.
Table~\ref{tab:size} repeats the ranking within quartiles of repository size (quartile
boundaries 73, 131 and 246 nodes; the largest repository has 2{,}487). The median of 131
graph nodes and the median of 286{,}385 tokens per repository are consistent: they imply
roughly 2{,}200 tokens, or some 260 lines, per file, which is an ordinary Python module.

The pattern of Table~\ref{tab:main} holds in every quartile, so the uncontrolled ranking is
not an artefact of repositories one can almost read whole. This analysis runs on the full
corpus without either control, so it says nothing about whether the qualifications of
Sections~\ref{sec:shared} and~\ref{sec:leak} are size-dependent; we report it as a robustness
check on Table~\ref{tab:main} alone. The gap does not widen monotonically with size: the
co-edited-minus-symbol rank gap for \m{ppr\_und\_pl} runs 9, 5, 9, 10 across the quartiles
and for \m{hops\_lines} 5, 1, 3, 3, so the right claim is stability, not a trend. In the
largest quartile, issue-text path matching is sixth on co-edited files and fifteenth on
symbol files, while length-aware personalised PageRank is twelfth and second respectively. The
query-independent prior degrades fastest of all: on co-edited files in the largest
quartile it scores 0.113 against a random floor of 0.087, which is to say that in the
repositories where retrieval matters most, knowing only which files are central is worth
almost nothing. \m{rrf\_hops\_path} never falls below sixth in any of the eight cells,
and is fourth or better in five of them.
