\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{What we can and cannot say about the two keys.} The tidy version of this paper
would be that the import graph answers the compiler's question and the issue text answers
the developer's, and that the field has been grading the first against the second. Our own
controls will not support the tidy version.

On the symbol key, structural methods win on the full corpus and are indistinguishable from
issue-to-path matching once the population is matched to the co-edited key
(Section~\ref{sec:shared}). That key is also built by following imports, so we would have
discounted a win there in any case. On the co-edited key, issue-to-path matching wins on the
full corpus and becomes indistinguishable from pure structure once tasks whose issues name a
key file in code are removed, losing to it only in the strictest stratum
(Section~\ref{sec:leak}). Each half of the reversal, in other words, has an
explanation that is not about the signals at all --- one is a population effect, the other a
leakage effect. The uncontrolled comparison reports both halves as findings about the
signals; the controlled comparison does not.

Calling the first of these an artefact would undersell it. Single-file pull requests are
454 of the 1{,}156 our symbol key covers, and they are real work, not a sampling accident.
What the matching control shows is that structure's advantage on the symbol key is
\emph{concentrated} in them: on those 454 the best directed walk scores 0.605 and the five
best non-oracle orderings are all structural, against 0.417 for the same walk on the matched population.
That is a finding in its own right, and an intuitive one --- when a change touches one file,
what it needs is most likely to be what that file imports. It is not evidence that structure
beats words in general, which is what the unmatched table appears to say.

A human-annotated key lets us say which proxy to believe where they disagree, and it sides
with the co-edited key (Section~\ref{sec:contextbench}). On ContextBench's tasks the length-aware
walks drop from second and fifth under the symbol key to eleventh and fifteenth under the
human one, and on the context a fix reads without editing --- the files a graph walk is meant
to surface --- walks and issue text are indistinguishable. The symbol key's preference for
structure is, on this evidence, largely a property of how that key is built.

What remains is weaker but real. The two keys still induce different rankings, and a method
tuned on one is not thereby good on the other. But the summary of the single-signal
comparison is that neither family dominates once both confounds are controlled, and the
interesting result is elsewhere.

\paragraph{Two effects, not one.} The result we would most like carried forward is
Section~\ref{sec:issue}, and its interest is that it separates two things the literature
reports as one number: filename leakage, which is causal and large, and a residual difference
between the issues that name files and those that do not, which no redaction we could define
removes. Both halves matter here. Ignore
the first and a lexical baseline looks stronger than it is; ignore the second and the
stratified comparison looks like proof that issue text does nothing, which our own
within-task experiment contradicts. We resist the second reading in particular: the null in
the no-mention stratum bounds the issue's contribution at about 0.03 AUC on 531 pull
requests. It does not show it is zero.

\paragraph{Fusion is the safe choice.} Reciprocal-rank fusion of a
length-aware walk with issue-to-path matching is the best non-oracle ordering under both keys
on the matched population, where it beats the best pure lexical ordering by 0.055 and 0.067
and the best pure structural one by 0.097 and 0.039 at the repository level. Across 200
random repository splits a mechanical criterion selects it on the choosing half in 198, and
in 195 of those it is the best non-oracle ordering on the half that did not choose it
(Section~\ref{sec:heldout}): the choice is stable across the repositories we have, which is
not the same as having been confirmed on repositories we do not.

The claim is robustness rather than dominance. Under the joint control of
Table~\ref{tab:leak} the fusion is first or second on co-edited files in every stratum, behind
only another fusion where it is not first, but sits behind two length-aware walks on symbol files
in the two stricter strata, by margins that do not survive correction
($p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$). On the matched population, in every leakage stratum and on either
key, the fusion is never significantly worse than the best pure ordering and is often
significantly better. On the full symbol-key population it is not: once the tasks whose issue
names a key file are removed, the length-aware walks beat it by 0.049 to 0.062
($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$), because that population keeps the 454 single-file pull
requests in which structure's advantage is concentrated. For a change that touches one file,
the walk alone is the better choice. That is what we would recommend on, and it is a weaker
claim than ``fusion wins''.

Three checks added in response to review bear on how far it travels. It is not an artefact of
the cost rule: under a rule that skips an oversized file instead of stopping, the fusion
remains best or within 0.003 of best, though the part of its margin owed to length-awareness
shrinks by about sixty per cent, and under a per-file rule the unscaled fusion is the one to
use (Section~\ref{sec:metric}). It is not an artefact of our keys: against a human-annotated
key it is second of twenty-two, 0.009 behind a fusion of the same family. And it does not
depend on being handed the file to change: when the issue's own best guess is used as the
seed, right in only 41\% of pull requests, walking from the guess and fusing still gives the
best non-oracle ordering under both keys (Section~\ref{sec:seedless}).

We were also able to test the obvious alternative explanation. The fusions are the only
methods given both the seed and the issue, so ``a fusion just gets more input'' is the null
for the whole result. The issue-free twins of Section~\ref{sec:issue} answer it: blending a
second list does help a little by itself --- \m{rrf\_pprpl\_seedpath} beats its own walk
\m{ppr\_und\_pl} by 0.049 on co-edited files --- but the issue-aware fusion beats the twin by
a further 0.065, both on the full corpus with the repository as the unit. Complementarity is
real, and between a third and seven tenths of what the issue adds to it is leakage: on the
matched population the issue is worth 0.069 to the fusion over all tasks, and the three
redaction arms cost 0.023, 0.043 and 0.048 of it.

\paragraph{The field's default key, restated carefully.} Every repository-context system in
Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys}, graph-based or not, is graded against the files the gold patch
touched --- our \m{co\_edited} source. On that source, and given a correct seed file, the best
purely structural ordering trails matching issue words against file paths by 0.039 AUC over
the full corpus ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.07$ with the repository as the unit; $< 10^{-3}$ in the
mixed model); once the issues naming a key file are removed the two are indistinguishable.
What matters for those evaluations is that the comparison depends on a property of the issue
corpus that none of them reports for its own evaluation.

Two further qualifications matter. Our main task hands every structural method a correct seed
file for free, whereas LocAgent, CoSIL and the rest must localize from the issue text alone.
Section~\ref{sec:seedless} removes the free seed in the simplest way --- the top file of an
issue-only lexical ranking becomes the seed --- and finds that the walk still adds to what the
issue alone retrieves, clearly on the symbol key and marginally on the edited files, but a
learned localiser inside an agent loop is a different component, and its graph may earn its
place differently. And they are LLM agents that also read the issue, so the graph is one
component among several. This paper is therefore not evidence about how well their graph
components perform in their own setting. What it shows is that, given a correct seed or the
issue's own guess at one, graph proximity is not the strongest single signal on the key those
systems adopt, and that the comparison depends on how often the issues name the files being
scored.

\paragraph{Naming the answer deserves to be a standard stratum.} Two tasks in five in this
corpus have an issue that names a key file as code. That is not a benchmark defect --- real
reports really do contain stack traces --- but it means any lexical baseline evaluated
without the stratification is reporting a mixture of two very different regimes, and any
structural method compared against such a baseline is being judged against a moving target.
The control costs a regular expression over text the benchmark already ships. We think
retrieval papers should report the rate and the stratified result as a matter of course, in
the same way they report the corpus size.

\paragraph{What ``within two hops'' is worth.} The two-hop neighbourhood earns its
reputation on recall and loses it on precision: it contains seven of every eight needed
files and also half the repository. Reporting the recall without the size is, on this
corpus, reporting half a statistic.

\paragraph{What this means for an agent's context, and what it does not.} The budget framing
is not decoration: at a median 286{,}385 tokens, most of these repositories do not fit in the
windows current systems run with, so selection is forced rather than optional. Two numbers
bound what selection can achieve. The answer is a median 2.98\% of the repository, so a
well-chosen context could be some 34$\times$ smaller than the whole; and an oracle ordering
fits the complete answer inside 8{,}000 lines for 97.5\% of pull requests where our best
method manages 58.5\%.

We do not show that better selection raises repair rates. We did not run an agent, and a retrieval improvement need not survive contact with one. What the ceiling
licenses is the weaker statement: a file absent from the context cannot be used, so the share
of tasks whose answer fits the budget bounds any system operating under it. It does not
license the claim that the remaining gap is reachable from the signals we have, only that it
is not closed off by the tasks themselves. Section~\ref{sec:protocol} specifies the
experiment that would convert the bound into a performance claim, in advance of running it.

\paragraph{A note on order versus selection.} An ordering plus a budget is a selection, and
it is the selection that matters here. We make no claim about the position of a file
\emph{within} a prompt, which is a different question with its own literature; every result
in this paper concerns which files are read at all.

\paragraph{The human reading of the same result.} The budget for a developer is attention
rather than tokens, and the results have a plain reading there. Asked to fix the login page,
a developer thinks of the authentication files partly because the words match and partly
because the imports connect; our fusion result says those two routes are largely
complementary, and our leakage result says that how much the words help depends on how
explicitly the report was written. We report the token framing because it makes the budget
concrete and measurable; we do not think the finding is confined to machines.

\paragraph{Recommendations.} (1) Report retrieval results separately for at least one
structural and one behavioural notion of relevance, and report the worst case across them.
(2) Report, and stratify by, whether the query text names the answer files in code.
(3) Match populations before comparing across keys; a key that only exists for multi-file
changes does not cover the same tasks as one that does not.
(4) Treat a query-independent repository prior, not random order, as the floor for
structural methods --- on symbol-style keys it reaches 83\% of a personalised walk's absolute
AUC, or 67\% of the walk's margin over a random ordering, which is the fairer reading.
(5) Where a graph-based tool orders context by structure alone, add a lexical signal from
the issue text and make the structural side length-aware before fusing; where one already
uses both, report them separately as well as combined.
(6) Report cost in tokens and report the ceiling alongside the score, so a reader can tell a
hard task from a poor ordering.
(7) Cluster paired tests by repository; pull requests within a repository are not
independent, and ignoring that overstates significance --- here 102 of 1{,}076 comparisons
significant by pull request are not significant by repository.
(8) Before attributing a gain to issue text, run the two controls of
Section~\ref{sec:issue}: delete the answer files' names from the issue and re-score the same
tasks, and compare against the same method with the issue replaced by a seed-derived query.
Redact more than the filenames: on our corpus deleting the names alone costs the best fusion
0.061 AUC, and deleting their directories and defined symbols too costs 0.096, so a
names-only redaction is a lower bound.

\section{A Protocol for the Downstream Test, Fixed in Advance}
\label{sec:protocol}

This paper measures retrieval, not repair. The obvious next question --- whether a context
assembled by one of these orderings lets a model actually fix the issue --- requires running
models, which we have not done. Rather than gesture at it as future work, we specify it here
in enough detail to be executed or contradicted, in the same spirit as the design freeze
that preceded this study (\S\ref{sec:design-freeze}). We commit to reporting the result
whichever way it falls.

\paragraph{Corpus.} The 1{,}162 scored pull requests of this study. Every one carries a
test specification from the benchmark suite it came from, naming the tests that must change
from failing to passing and those that must keep passing, so resolution can be decided by
execution rather than by patch similarity. We note that only 15 of them overlap SWE-bench Verified, so this is not a
re-run of an existing leaderboard.

\begin{sloppypar}
\paragraph{Conditions.} Eight contexts per task, each truncated to the same token budget. A
repair experiment has no evidence key --- the model gets one context and either the tests pass
or they do not --- so every condition names one concrete ordering:
(i) the seed file alone, a floor;
(ii) seed plus \m{ppr\_und\_pl}, the structural input of the recommended fusion (iv), so that
(ii) against (iv) isolates what the issue adds downstream;
(iii) seed plus \m{path\_issue}, the best lexical ordering;
(iv) seed plus \m{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path}, the best fusion on the matched population and the
one confirmed on held-out repositories;
(v) seed plus \m{rrf\_hops\_path}, the best fusion by worst-case rank, carried as well because
the two criteria select different fusions and we will not choose between them after the fact;
(vi) seed plus \m{rrf\_pprpl\_seedpath}, the issue-free twin of (iv), so that the downstream
test inherits the control of Section~\ref{sec:issue};
(vii) the repository truncated to the budget in a fixed canonical order, which is what a
system with no retrieval step does;
(viii) seed plus the key files themselves, cheapest first --- the \m{oracle} ordering, an upper
reference used to calibrate the budget, not a contender. Budgets of 16{,}000 and 64{,}000 tokens, chosen
from Table~\ref{tab:ceiling} to sit either side of the point where most answers begin to
fit.
\end{sloppypar}

\paragraph{Models.} Two, of clearly different capability, so that the result is not a
property of one model. A weak model that fails everywhere and a strong model that succeeds
everywhere would both be uninformative; the pilot below exists to detect that before the
full run.

\paragraph{Generation.} A single API call per task and condition, with no tools and no
retrieval available to the model. This is essential rather than incidental: a model that can
search the repository defeats the budget, and the quantity under study is what a fixed
context supports.

\paragraph{Outcome and analysis.} A task is resolved if the generated patch applies and the
specified tests pass. The comparison is paired across conditions on the same tasks, tested
with McNemar's test, Holm-corrected across the condition pairs. Because pull requests cluster
within repositories, the primary analysis is a mixed-effects logistic regression with a random
intercept per repository and condition as a fixed effect, with the McNemar result reported
alongside; this follows the unit argument of Section~\ref{sec:stats} rather than the
pull-request-level convention we abandoned there. We do not require the models to be reliable; we require the
\emph{difference between conditions} to be measurable, and the pairing makes the stochastic
component common to all conditions.

\paragraph{Pilot and stopping rule.} A 150-task pilot on the weaker model precedes the full
run. If the oracle condition (viii) resolves under 10\% or over 90\% of pilot tasks, the budget is
outside the informative range and is adjusted before the main run --- and that adjustment is
reported.

\paragraph{What would falsify the implication.} If conditions (ii) to (vi) do not differ from
(vii) at equal budget, then retrieval quality does not transfer to repair at these budgets,
and the results of this paper should be read as being about retrieval alone. If (iv) does not
beat (vi), the issue text does not earn its place downstream either, which would extend
Section~\ref{sec:issue} from retrieval to repair. Both outcomes are publishable and we would
report them.

\section{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{Construct.} Neither evidence source is ground truth about what a developer needed
to read; they are recoverable proxies with opposite biases, which is why we report both and
never merge them. The co-edited key in particular conflates files that were \emph{changed}
with files that had to be \emph{read}, and the symbol key is built by a resolver that follows
import edges, so it is partly circular with the structural methods it favours; the
human-annotated key of Section~\ref{sec:contextbench} confirms that its preference for
structure does not carry over. That key has limits of its own: it covers 108 pull requests,
most from SWE-bench Verified repositories that are heavily studied, and its annotators worked
from the fix, so it records what the fix needed rather than what a developer consulted. Coverage per line assumes whole files are read, which overstates the cost
for agents that read selectively; Section~\ref{sec:metric} shows which conclusions depend on
that accounting. The execution-based source is absent (Section~\ref{sec:keys}) and would be
the natural third leg.

\paragraph{Internal.} The graph builder resolves imports statically and misses dynamic
imports and plugin registration. The symbol key is produced by a static analyser and
inherits its resolution failures, and those failures depend on the environment the analyser
runs in: rebuilding every key on a second machine left all 1{,}886 co-edited keys identical but
changed the symbol key of 41 pull requests, usually by one file. Re-scoring with the rebuilt
keys moves no AUC by more than 0.003, swaps two adjacent orderings 0.0003 apart, and changes
no conclusion; it does move some quoted figures in the third decimal, and the held-out counts
of Section~\ref{sec:heldout} to 194 and 191 of 200. The paper reports the keys as first built;
the replication package records every key that differs and the re-scored comparison. Both biases favour structural methods. Issue-path leakage is
measured and does substantially drive the co-edited result: it is reported in
Section~\ref{sec:leak} as a finding rather than a reassurance, and the corresponding claim
is stated conditionally throughout. Our leakage classifier is a regular expression over
issue text and will mislabel some mentions in either direction; we report three nested
strata, and three nested redaction arms, rather than one of each, so that the conclusion does
not rest on a single cut. Leakage we have not thought to redact --- a paraphrase of a function's
behaviour, a quoted error message defined in a key file --- would sit in the residual that
Section~\ref{sec:issue} does not attribute to leakage, so the leakage share is bounded below
more firmly than above.

\paragraph{External.} Python only, file granularity only, and pull requests drawn from
benchmark suites that select for reproducible test-verified fixes --- a population plausibly
better documented than average, which may flatter the issue-text methods. The median
repository here has 131 graph files and very large repositories are under-represented. The
size split in Section~\ref{sec:size} runs on the uncontrolled corpus, so it shows only
that the pattern of Table~\ref{tab:main} is stable across size quartiles rather than
widening with size; it is not a size effect, but we cannot show the bias is harmless.

\paragraph{Conclusion.} Pull-request-level aggregation, repository-level paired tests, Holm
correction within comparison families and bootstrapping over repositories guard against the
main inflation risks. Effect sizes accompany every test because several differences are
significant and small. The fusion family, the worst-rank criterion and the directed walks
were all added after the design freeze, so they are exploratory in origin;
Section~\ref{sec:heldout} shows the selection is stable across resamples of our
repositories, and Section~\ref{sec:external} that it holds, at the margin we allowed, on seven
repositories outside the sample under predictions fixed in advance. Neither addresses the fact
that the family was chosen after seeing results, and seven repositories are a small external
set: one of the four predictions failed on it.

\section{Conclusion}

Given the file being changed, what else belongs in an agent's context? Import-graph proximity
and issue-text matching answer differently, and under two defensible definitions of the answer
they appear to trade places. That reversal is mostly the comparison, not the signals: one half
is the different pull requests the two keys cover, the other the issues that name their files.

What remains is two findings. Issue-aware retrieval is worth far more when the issue names a
file the change touches, and between 0.061 and 0.078 of that 0.140 advantage is the naming
itself; a benchmark average over issues that do and do not name their files describes neither,
and should be reported per regime. And reciprocal-rank fusion of a length-aware walk with
issue-to-path matching is the robust choice --- never significantly worse than the best single
signal on the pull requests carrying both keys, stable across repository splits, and holding
on seven repositories outside the sample --- except for single-file changes, where the walk
alone is better. It costs a BM25 index over file paths and contents.

We recommend that context-retrieval work for code change report per evidence source, report
and stratify by whether the query names the answer, compare any issue-aware method against
the same method with a seed-derived query, match populations before comparing across keys,
cluster its tests by repository, and use a repository prior rather than random order as its
floor.

\section*{Data Availability}

The replication package contains the import graphs at every base commit, the task
definitions and evidence keys, the issue-token bags, the per-task orderings and coverage
curves, the per-file token counts, and the analysis scripts that produce every number and
figure in this paper; the external and ContextBench trees with their pre-registrations, which
the version history shows were committed before the data they concern were scored; and the
script that computes the dense embeddings, which are regenerated rather than shipped. A
checker recomputes every number quoted in the text from the result files and fails if any
sentence disagrees with them. It is available to reviewers at submission, and will be archived at a
permanent identifier on acceptance.

\section*{Use of AI Tools}

Claude (Anthropic) was used to write the analysis and method code, to run the experiments
and to draft this manuscript. All numeric results are produced by scripts in the replication
package and were copied mechanically from their output files; the author verified the
design, the claims and the text. Bibliographic entries were drafted with AI assistance and
then checked against arXiv, the ACL Anthology and the publisher listings on 2026-09-23; the
evaluation section of every system in Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys} was read directly rather
than summarised from an abstract. That check corrected eight entries drafted from memory,
including a journal name, an author order, three titles changed between preprint versions,
and one volume recorded as authored that is in fact edited. The corrections are listed in
the replication package.

\section{Correction Families and Mixed-Model Estimates}
